title: John Lennon live: John Sinclair Freedom Rally, Crisler Arena, Ann Arbor | 1971
content:
John Lennon and Yoko Ono performed at the John Sinclair Freedom Rally, held at the Crisler Arena in Ann Arbor, Michigan, on 10 December 1971.

The rally was in support of American writer and political activist John Sinclair, who had been arrested and given a 10-year prison sentence in 1969 for distribution of marijuana. The sentence was widely condemned as unduly harsh, and led to a number of high-profile protests.

The John Sinclair Freedom Rally was attended by 15,000 people. The musical performers included Lennon and Ono, Phil Ochs, The Up, Commander Cody and His Lost Planet Airmen, Bob Seger, Stevie Wonder, Archie Shepp, Joy Of Cooking, David Peel, and Teegarden & Van Winkle. Speakers included Bobby Seale, Jerry Rubin, Allen Ginsberg, Rennie Davis, James Groppi, Sheila Murphy, Johnnie Tillmon, Ed Sanders, and Jane Fonda.

The rally lasted into the night, and the Plastic Ono Lower East Side took to the stage shortly after 3am the following morning, more than two hours behind schedule. The band included guitarists Chris Osborne, Eddie Mottau, David Peel, and members of the Lower East Side: Billy Minelli, Frank Lanci, and Tom Doyle. Also on stage during the set were Apple Corps’ promotions man Toby Morris, and activists Leslie Bacon, Lenox Raphael, and Jerry Rubin.

They performed four songs, all of which appeared on the 1972 album Some Time In New York City: ‘Attica State’, ‘The Luck Of The Irish’, ‘Sisters, O Sisters’, and ‘John Sinclair’. The performance was filmed, and included in the short film Ten For Two.

Ono introduced ‘Sisters, O Sisters’ by announcing that she “wrote this song the day before yesterday for sisters in Ann Arbor, Michigan”. Lennon had also written ‘John Sinclair’ especially for the event. Its chorus included the line “They gave him ten for two”, a reference to Sinclair’s 10-year prison sentence for the possession of 11.50 grains of marijuana – around two joints’ worth.

Lennon had agreed to perform after being asked by activist Jerry Rubin. John Sinclair’s wife Leni and music events promoter Peter Andrews flew to New York City to meet Lennon and Ono at their West Village apartment.

They greeted us, they were very friendly, very, very nice. I had Lennon sign a contract for $500 to appear, and he crossed it out and put, ‘To be donated to the John Sinclair Freedom Fund.’

He wasn’t sure if the song was appropriate, and he wanted my opinion. He sang the song – ‘It ain’t fair, John Sinclair’ – with that steel guitar he had. I assured him it was totally appropriate, and the lyrics were cool. He was very grateful

I thought to myself, ‘John Lennon’s asking my opinion! Man, this is somethin’ else.

Peter Andrews
Ann Arbor Chronicle, 27 December 2009

Andrews also recorded a message from Lennon to help promote the event: “Hello, this is John with Yoko here. I just want to say we’re coming along to the John Sinclair bust fund rally to say hello. I won’t be bringing a band or nothing like that because I’m only here as a tourist, but I’ll probably fetch me guitar, and I know we have a song that we wrote for John. So that’s that.”

Tickets went on sale for $3 on 8 December, just two days before the rally, and sold out in a matter of hours. No money was spent on advertising; the media attention caused by Lennon’s appearance was enough.

John Sinclair was released from prison on 13 December 1971, three days after the rally, after the Michigan Supreme Court ruled that the state’s marijuana statutes were unconstitutional.
